Entropy-Regularized Dynamic Programming

Infinite-horizon dynamic programming selects actions with a hard maximum. That operator is nondifferentiable at ties and produces a deterministic greedy choice. Can a modified control objective produce both a smooth Bellman operator and a stochastic optimal policy? Convex regularization supplies the link.

While the standard Bellman optimality equations use the max operator to determine the best action, an alternative formulation known as the smooth or soft Bellman optimality equations replaces it with a smooth approximation of the maximum. The history of these equations runs across two communities that rarely read each other. They appear in the work of the structural econometrician John Rust on the replacement of bus engines Rust (1987), together with an inverse problem and an algorithm to solve it. Ng & Russell (2000), who are usually credited with introducing inverse reinforcement learning, cite Rust, but the connection was then largely lost. Ziebart et al. (2008) rediscovered the same equations as maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning, named after the maximum entropy principle. Haarnoja et al. (2017) built on Ziebart to obtain soft Q-learning, and soft actor-critic Haarnoja et al. (2018), one of the most widely used deep RL algorithms for continuous control, followed a year later.

In the infinite-horizon setting, the smooth Bellman optimality equations take the form:

vβ⋆(s)=1βlog⁡∑a∈Asexp⁡(β(r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)vβ⋆(j)))v^\star_\beta(s) = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp\left(\beta\left(r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j | s, a) v^\star_\beta(j)\right)\right)vβ⋆​(s)=β1​loga∈As​∑​exp⎝⎛​β⎝⎛​r(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)vβ⋆​(j)⎠⎞​⎠⎞​
(1)

We write vβ⋆v^\star_\betavβ⋆​ for this smooth value function, to keep it apart from the optimal value vγ∗v^*_\gammavγ∗​ of the hard Bellman equation.

Adopting an operator-theoretic perspective, we can define a nonlinear operator Lβ\mathrm{L}_\betaLβ​ such that the smooth value function of an MDP is then the solution to the following fixed-point equation:

(Lβv)(s)=1βlog⁡∑a∈Asexp⁡(β(r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)v(j)))(\mathrm{L}_\beta \mathbf{v})(s) = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp\left(\beta\left(r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v(j)\right)\right)(Lβ​v)(s)=β1​loga∈As​∑​exp⎝⎛​β⎝⎛​r(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)v(j)⎠⎞​⎠⎞​
(2)

As β→∞\beta \to \inftyβ→∞, Lβ\mathrm{L}_\betaLβ​ converges to the standard Bellman operator L\BellmanL. Furthermore, it can be shown that the smooth Bellman operator is a contraction mapping in the supremum norm, and therefore has a unique fixed point. However, as opposed to the usual “hard” setting, the fixed point of Lβ\mathrm{L}_\betaLβ​ is associated with the value function of an optimal stochastic policy defined by the softmax distribution:

π(a∣s)=exp⁡(β(r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)vβ⋆(j)))∑a′∈Asexp⁡(β(r(s,a′)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a′)vβ⋆(j)))\pi(a|s) = \frac{\exp\left(\beta\left(r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v^\star_\beta(j)\right)\right)}{\sum_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp\left(\beta\left(r(s,a') + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a') v^\star_\beta(j)\right)\right)}π(a∣s)=∑a′∈As​​exp(β(r(s,a′)+γ∑j∈S​p(j∣s,a′)vβ⋆​(j)))exp(β(r(s,a)+γ∑j∈S​p(j∣s,a)vβ⋆​(j)))​
(3)

Despite the confusing terminology, the above “softmax” policy is the smooth counterpart of the argmax in the original optimality equation, not of the max: it is a soft-argmax. The smooth counterpart of the max is the log-sum-exp. The same policy is also called a Boltzmann or Gibbs policy. As the temperature 1/β1/\beta1/β goes to zero, the softmax concentrates on the maximizing actions and we recover the greedy policy and the hard Bellman equation.

Stochastic Policies: Exploration and the Partition Function¶

Moving from the argmax to the softmax turns deterministic policies into stochastic ones, which is both useful and costly. It is useful because noise in the actions is a way to explore. In RL the agent usually gathers its own data, and if it always took the action it currently believes best it would never learn about the others. The problem is not specific to RL. An engineer identifying a model of a plant must also choose inputs that reveal the dynamics, and in system identification this is called exciting the system: a persistently exciting input is one rich enough for the parameters to be identifiable from the data.

It is costly when the action set is continuous. The softmax policy is then a density π(a∣s)∝exp⁡(βq(s,a))\pi(a \mid s) \propto \exp(\beta q(s,a))π(a∣s)∝exp(βq(s,a)) whose normalizing constant, the partition function ∫exp⁡(βq(s,a)) da\int \exp(\beta q(s,a))\, da∫exp(βq(s,a))da, is an integral with no closed form in general. The log-sum-exp value has the same problem, since it is the logarithm of that integral. This is the intractable partition function familiar from energy-based models and probabilistic graphical models. Numerical quadrature is an option in low dimension but is rarely used. Haarnoja et al. (2017) sampled from the softmax policy over continuous actions with amortized Stein variational gradient descent, which proved expensive; soft actor-critic Haarnoja et al. (2018) instead fits a tractable parametric policy to the softmax, an idea we return to in the chapters on fitted value methods and policy learning. The notation for continuous actions, and what changes when sums become integrals, is in Continuous Action and State Spaces.

This formulation is interesting for several reasons. First, smoothness is a desirable property from an optimization standpoint. Unlike γ\gammaγ, we view β\betaβ as a hyperparameter of our algorithm, which we can control to achieve the desired level of accuracy.

Second, we presented the equations pragmatically, by replacing the max with the log-sum-exp (a smooth maximum) and the argmax with the softmax (a smooth argmax). The same equations come out of two other starting points, and this chapter follows all three routes:

  1. Smoothing the operator. Replace every max by a log-sum-exp, as above. This is the route of the next subsection, and the justification is computational: a smooth operator has gradients everywhere.

  2. Noise on the rewards. Keep the hard Bellman equation, but suppose that each action’s reward is perturbed by independent Gumbel noise that the decision maker sees and the modeler does not. Integrating the noise out gives the log-sum-exp (Gumbel Noise on the Rewards). This is how Rust (1987) motivated the equations, following the discrete choice models of econometrics.

  3. Entropy regularization. Keep the rewards, but add a bonus proportional to the entropy of the policy in every state. The regularized Bellman equation is again the log-sum-exp equation (Regularized Markov Decision Processes). This is the reading behind maximum entropy RL and soft actor-critic.

Each route brings its own tools: smoothness gives differentiability, the noise model gives a likelihood for observed behavior, and the regularization view gives convex duality. A fourth reading, close to the third, starts from the energy-based models of supervised learning, where a softmax turns unnormalized scores into a distribution; this is essentially what Ziebart et al. (2008) did. It connects to probabilistic graphical models, where finding an optimal smooth policy becomes an inference problem. This is the idea of control as inference, whose converse, inference as control, is now used to derive samplers and amortized inference methods with RL Levine et al. (2018).

Smooth Value Iteration Algorithm¶

Before iterating Lβ\mathrm{L}_\betaLβ​, we should check that iterating it is the right thing to do, that is, that it is a contraction. It is, in the sup-norm and with the same factor γ\gammaγ as the hard Bellman operator. The proof uses the same three facts as for L\BellmanL. The log-sum-exp is monotone, it commutes with adding a constant to all of its arguments, and Lβ\mathrm{L}_\betaLβ​ maps a uniform shift c1c\mathbf{1}c1 of vvv into a shift γc1\gamma c\mathbf{1}γc1 of Lβv\mathrm{L}_\beta vLβ​v. From v≤u+∥v−u∥∞1v \le u + \|v-u\|_\infty\mathbf{1}v≤u+∥v−u∥∞​1 we get Lβv≤Lβu+γ∥v−u∥∞1\mathrm{L}_\beta v \le \mathrm{L}_\beta u + \gamma\|v-u\|_\infty\mathbf{1}Lβ​v≤Lβ​u+γ∥v−u∥∞​1, and exchanging uuu and vvv gives the contraction. A word of caution about the converse: failing to show that an operator is a contraction does not mean that its fixed point fails to exist or that no algorithm finds it. Contraction is a convenient sufficient condition, and other fixed-point theorems cover other cases.

Successive approximation applied to Lβ\mathrm{L}_\betaLβ​ is smooth value iteration. It has the structure of value iteration, with a log-sum-exp wherever value iteration had a max and a softmax policy at the end where value iteration returned a greedy one.

(4)

and the softmax policy returned by the algorithm loses at most ε+log⁡∣A∣β(1−γ)\varepsilon + \frac{\log|\mathcal{A}|}{\beta(1-\gamma)}ε+β(1−γ)log∣A∣​ against the optimal value of the unregularized MDP. The temperature therefore adds a bias that does not shrink with more iterations; it is the price of smoothness and of exploration.

Gumbel Noise on the Rewards¶

Why does adding independent Gumbel perturbations to action rewards produce a log-sum-exp value before the perturbation is observed?

We can obtain the smooth Bellman equation by considering a setting in which we have Gumbel noise added to the reward function. This derivation provides theoretical insight and also connects to practical modeling scenarios where rewards have random perturbations.

Step 1: Define the Augmented MDP with Gumbel Noise¶

At each time period and state sss, we draw an action-indexed shock vector:

ϵt(s)=(ϵt(s,a))a∈As,where ϵt(s,a) i.i.d.∼Gumbel(μϵ,1/β)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t(s) = \big(\epsilon_t(s,a)\big)_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s}, \quad \text{where } \epsilon_t(s,a) \text{ i.i.d.} \sim \mathrm{Gumbel}(\mu_\epsilon, 1/\beta)ϵt​(s)=(ϵt​(s,a))a∈As​​,where ϵt​(s,a) i.i.d.∼Gumbel(μϵ​,1/β)
(5)

These shocks are independent across time periods, states, and actions, and are independent of the MDP transition dynamics p(⋅∣s,a)p(\cdot | s, a)p(⋅∣s,a).

The Gumbel distribution with location parameter μ\muμ and scale parameter 1/β1/\beta1/β has probability density function:

f(x;μ,1/β)=βexp⁡(−β(x−μ)−exp⁡(−β(x−μ)))f(x; \mu, 1/\beta) = \beta\exp\left(-\beta(x-\mu)-\exp(-\beta(x-\mu))\right)f(x;μ,1/β)=βexp(−β(x−μ)−exp(−β(x−μ)))
(6)

To generate a Gumbel-distributed random variable, we can use inverse transform sampling: X=μ−1βlog⁡(−log⁡(U))X = \mu - \frac{1}{\beta} \log(-\log(U))X=μ−β1​log(−log(U)) where UUU is uniform on (0,1)(0,1)(0,1).

Zero-Mean Shocks

To ensure the shocks have zero mean, we set μϵ=−γE/β\mu_\epsilon = -\gamma_E/\betaμϵ​=−γE​/β where γE≈0.5772\gamma_E \approx 0.5772γE​≈0.5772 is the Euler-Mascheroni constant. This choice eliminates an additive constant that would otherwise appear in the smooth Bellman equation. For simplicity, we will adopt this convention throughout.

We now define an augmented MDP with:

  • Augmented state: s~=(s,ϵ)\tilde{s} = (s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon})s~=(s,ϵ) where s∈Ss \in \mathcal{S}s∈S and ϵ∈R∣As∣\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{A}_s|}ϵ∈R∣As​∣

  • Augmented reward: r~(s~,a)=r(s,a)+ϵ(a)\tilde{r}(\tilde{s}, a) = r(s,a) + \epsilon(a)r~(s~,a)=r(s,a)+ϵ(a)

  • Augmented transition: p~(s~′∣s~,a)=p(s′∣s,a)⋅p(ϵ′)\tilde{p}(\tilde{s}' | \tilde{s}, a) = p(s' | s, a) \cdot p(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}')p~​(s~′∣s~,a)=p(s′∣s,a)⋅p(ϵ′)

The transition factorizes because the next shock vector ϵ′\boldsymbol{\epsilon}'ϵ′ is drawn independently of the current state and action (conditional independence).

The Augmented State Space is Uncountable

Even if the original state space S\mathcal{S}S and action space A\mathcal{A}A are finite, the augmented state space S~=S×R∣A∣\tilde{\mathcal{S}} = \mathcal{S} \times \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{A}|}S~=S×R∣A∣ is uncountably infinite because each shock vector ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}ϵ is a continuous random variable. The space has finite dimension, ∣A∣|\mathcal{A}|∣A∣ coordinates for the shocks, but a value function on it is an element of an infinite-dimensional function space. The shocks are also unbounded, so the rewards r(s,a)+ϵ(a)r(s,a)+\epsilon(a)r(s,a)+ϵ(a) are unbounded and the sup-norm theory of the previous chapter does not apply as stated. Nothing breaks, because the shocks have finite mean and enter additively, but it is one more reason not to work on this space directly. Therefore:

  • We cannot enumerate the augmented states

  • Tabular dynamic programming methods do not apply directly

  • The augmented value function v~(s,ϵ)\tilde{v}(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon})v~(s,ϵ) maps a continuous space to R\mathbb{R}R

This motivates why we immediately marginalize over the shocks to obtain a finite-dimensional representation.

Step 2: The Hard Bellman Equation on the Augmented State Space¶

The Bellman optimality equation for the augmented MDP is:

v~(s,ϵ)=max⁡a∈As{r(s,a)+ϵ(a)+γEs′,ϵ′[v~(s′,ϵ′)∣s,a]}\tilde{v}(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{ r(s,a) + \epsilon(a) + \gamma \mathbb{E}_{s', \boldsymbol{\epsilon}'}\left[\tilde{v}(s', \boldsymbol{\epsilon}') \mid s, a\right] \right\}v~(s,ϵ)=a∈As​max​{r(s,a)+ϵ(a)+γEs′,ϵ′​[v~(s′,ϵ′)∣s,a]}
(7)

Here the expectation is over the next augmented state (s′,ϵ′)(s', \boldsymbol{\epsilon}')(s′,ϵ′), which includes both the next state s′∼p(⋅∣s,a)s' \sim p(\cdot | s, a)s′∼p(⋅∣s,a) and the next shock vector ϵ′∼p(⋅)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}' \sim p(\cdot)ϵ′∼p(⋅).

This is a perfectly well-defined Bellman equation, and an optimal stationary policy exists:

π(s,ϵ)∈argmax⁡a∈As{r(s,a)+ϵ(a)+γEs′,ϵ′[v~(s′,ϵ′)∣s,a]}\pi(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) \in \operatorname{argmax}_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{ r(s,a) + \epsilon(a) + \gamma \mathbb{E}_{s', \boldsymbol{\epsilon}'}\left[\tilde{v}(s', \boldsymbol{\epsilon}') \mid s, a\right] \right\}π(s,ϵ)∈argmaxa∈As​​{r(s,a)+ϵ(a)+γEs′,ϵ′​[v~(s′,ϵ′)∣s,a]}
(8)

However, this equation is computationally intractable because:

  • The state space is continuous (uncountable), so v~\tilde vv~ is a function on a continuum

  • The shocks are fresh each period

  • We would need to solve for v~\tilde{v}v~ over an uncountable domain

We never solve this equation directly. Instead, we use it as a mathematical device to derive the smooth Bellman equation.

Step 3: Define the Ex-Ante (Inclusive) Value Function¶

The idea here is to consider the expected value before observing the current shocks. We define what some authors in econometrics call the inclusive value or ex-ante value:

v(s):=Eϵ[v~(s,ϵ)]v(s) := \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\big[\tilde{v}(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon})\big]v(s):=Eϵ​[v~(s,ϵ)]
(9)

This is the value of being in state sss before we observe the current-period shock vector ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}ϵ.

Two Different Value Functions

It is crucial to distinguish:

  • v~(s,ϵ)\tilde{v}(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon})v~(s,ϵ): the value after observing shocks (conditional on ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}ϵ), defined on the augmented state space

  • v(s)v(s)v(s): the value before observing shocks (marginalizing over ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}ϵ), defined on the original state space

The function v(s)v(s)v(s) is what we actually compute and care about. The augmented value v~\tilde{v}v~ exists only as a proof device.

Step 4: Separate the Deterministic and Random Components¶

Now we take the expectation of the augmented Bellman equation with respect to the current shocks only (everything that does not depend on the current ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}ϵ can be pulled out).

First, note that by the law of iterated expectations and independence of shocks across time:

Eϵ′[v~(s′,ϵ′)]=v(s′)\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}'}\big[\tilde{v}(s', \boldsymbol{\epsilon}')\big] = v(s')Eϵ′​[v~(s′,ϵ′)]=v(s′)
(10)

This follows from our definition of vvv and the fact that the next shock is independent of everything else.

Now define the deterministic part of the right-hand side:

xa(s):=r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)v(j)x_a(s) := r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v(j)xa​(s):=r(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)v(j)
(11)

This is the expected return from taking action aaa in state sss without the shock. Using this notation, the augmented Bellman equation becomes:

v~(s,ϵ)=max⁡a∈As{xa(s)+ϵ(a)}\tilde{v}(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{ x_a(s) + \epsilon(a) \right\}v~(s,ϵ)=a∈As​max​{xa​(s)+ϵ(a)}
(12)

Taking the expectation over ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}ϵ on both sides:

v(s)=Eϵ[max⁡a∈As{xa(s)+ϵ(a)}]v(s) = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{ x_a(s) + \epsilon(a) \right\}\right]v(s)=Eϵ​[a∈As​max​{xa​(s)+ϵ(a)}]
(13)
Expectation of a Max, Not Max of an Expectation

Notice carefully: we have E[max⁡(⋅)]\mathbb{E}[\max(\cdot)]E[max(⋅)], not max⁡E[⋅]\max \mathbb{E}[\cdot]maxE[⋅]. We are not swapping max and expectation.

The expression Eϵ[max⁡a{xa+ϵ(a)}]\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}[\max_a \{x_a + \epsilon(a)\}]Eϵ​[maxa​{xa​+ϵ(a)}] is the expected value of the maximum of Gumbel-perturbed utilities. The Gumbel random utility identity evaluates this quantity in closed form.

Step 5: Apply the Gumbel Random Utility Identity¶

We now invoke a result from extreme value theory:

Lemma 1 (Gumbel Random Utility Identity)

Let ϵ1,…,ϵm\epsilon_1, \ldots, \epsilon_mϵ1​,…,ϵm​ be i.i.d. Gumbel(μϵ,1/β)\mathrm{Gumbel}(\mu_\epsilon, 1/\beta)Gumbel(μϵ​,1/β) random variables. For any deterministic values x1,…,xm∈Rx_1, \ldots, x_m \in \mathbb{R}x1​,…,xm​∈R:

max⁡i=1,…,m{xi+ϵi}=d1βlog⁡∑i=1mexp⁡(βxi)+ζ\max_{i=1,\ldots,m} \{x_i + \epsilon_i\} \overset{d}{=} \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{i=1}^m \exp(\beta x_i) + \zetai=1,…,mmax​{xi​+ϵi​}=dβ1​logi=1∑m​exp(βxi​)+ζ
(14)

where ζ∼Gumbel(μϵ,1/β)\zeta \sim \mathrm{Gumbel}(\mu_\epsilon, 1/\beta)ζ∼Gumbel(μϵ​,1/β) (same distribution as the original shocks).

Taking expectations:

E[max⁡i=1,…,m{xi+ϵi}]=1βlog⁡∑i=1mexp⁡(βxi)+μϵ+γEβ\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i=1,\ldots,m} \{x_i + \epsilon_i\}\right] = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{i=1}^m \exp(\beta x_i) + \mu_\epsilon + \frac{\gamma_E}{\beta}E[i=1,…,mmax​{xi​+ϵi​}]=β1​logi=1∑m​exp(βxi​)+μϵ​+βγE​​
(15)

where γE≈0.5772\gamma_E \approx 0.5772γE​≈0.5772 is the Euler-Mascheroni constant.

With mean-zero shocks (μϵ=−γE/β\mu_\epsilon = -\gamma_E/\betaμϵ​=−γE​/β), the constant term vanishes:

E[max⁡i=1,…,m{xi+ϵi}]=1βlog⁡∑i=1mexp⁡(βxi)\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i=1,\ldots,m} \{x_i + \epsilon_i\}\right] = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{i=1}^m \exp(\beta x_i)E[i=1,…,mmax​{xi​+ϵi​}]=β1​logi=1∑m​exp(βxi​)
(16)

Applying this identity to our problem (with mean-zero shocks):

v(s)=Eϵ[max⁡a∈As{xa(s)+ϵ(a)}]=1βlog⁡∑a∈Asexp⁡(βxa(s))v(s) = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \{x_a(s) + \epsilon(a)\}\right] = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp(\beta x_a(s))v(s)=Eϵ​[a∈As​max​{xa​(s)+ϵ(a)}]=β1​loga∈As​∑​exp(βxa​(s))
(17)

Substituting the definition of xa(s)x_a(s)xa​(s):

v(s)=1βlog⁡∑a∈Asexp⁡(β(r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)v(j)))v(s) = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp\left(\beta\left(r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v(j)\right)\right)v(s)=β1​loga∈As​∑​exp⎝⎛​β⎝⎛​r(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)v(j)⎠⎞​⎠⎞​
(18)

We have arrived at the smooth Bellman equation.

Step 6: Summary of the Derivation¶

To recap the logical flow:

  1. We constructed an augmented MDP with state (s,ϵ)(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon})(s,ϵ) where shocks perturb rewards

  2. We wrote the standard Bellman equation for this augmented MDP (hard max, but over an uncountable state space)

  3. We defined the ex-ante value v(s)=Eϵ[v~(s,ϵ)]v(s) = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}[\tilde{v}(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon})]v(s)=Eϵ​[v~(s,ϵ)] to eliminate the continuous shock component

  4. We separated deterministic and random terms: v~(s,ϵ)=max⁡a{xa(s)+ϵ(a)}\tilde{v}(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \max_a \{x_a(s) + \epsilon(a)\}v~(s,ϵ)=maxa​{xa​(s)+ϵ(a)}

  5. We applied the Gumbel identity to evaluate Eϵ[max⁡a{⋯ }]\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}[\max_a \{\cdots\}]Eϵ​[maxa​{⋯}] in closed form as a log-sum-exp

The augmented MDP with shocks exists only as a mathematical device. We never approximate v~\tilde{v}v~, never discretize ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}ϵ, and never enumerate the augmented state space. The only computational object we work with is v(s)v(s)v(s) on the original (finite) state space, which satisfies the smooth Bellman equation.

Deriving the Optimal Smooth Policy¶

Now that we have derived the smooth value function, we can also obtain the corresponding optimal policy. The question is: what policy should we follow in the original MDP (without explicitly conditioning on shocks)?

In the augmented MDP, the optimal policy is deterministic but depends on the shock realization:

π(s,ϵ)∈argmax⁡a∈As{r(s,a)+ϵ(a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)v(j)}\pi(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) \in \operatorname{argmax}_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{ r(s,a) + \epsilon(a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v(j) \right\}π(s,ϵ)∈argmaxa∈As​​⎩⎨⎧​r(s,a)+ϵ(a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)v(j)⎭⎬⎫​
(19)

However, we want a policy for the original state space sss (not the augmented state). We obtain this by marginalizing over the current shocks, essentially asking: “what is the probability that action aaa is optimal when we average over all possible shock realizations?”

Define an indicator function:

Ia(ϵ)={1if a∈argmax⁡a′∈As{xa′(s)+ϵ(a′)}0otherwiseI_a(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } a \in \operatorname{argmax}_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{ x_{a'}(s) + \epsilon(a') \right\} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}Ia​(ϵ)={10​if a∈argmaxa′∈As​​{xa′​(s)+ϵ(a′)}otherwise​
(20)

where xa(s)=r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)v(j)x_a(s) = r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v(j)xa​(s)=r(s,a)+γ∑j∈S​p(j∣s,a)v(j) as before.

The ex-ante probability that action aaa is optimal at state sss is:

π(a∣s)=Eϵ[Ia(ϵ)]=Pϵ(a∈argmax⁡a′{xa′(s)+ϵ(a′)})\pi(a|s) = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}[I_a(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})] = \mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left(a \in \operatorname{argmax}_{a'} \left\{ x_{a'}(s) + \epsilon(a') \right\}\right)π(a∣s)=Eϵ​[Ia​(ϵ)]=Pϵ​(a∈argmaxa′​{xa′​(s)+ϵ(a′)})
(21)

This is the probability that action aaa achieves the maximum when utilities are perturbed by Gumbel noise.

Lemma 2 (Gumbel-Max Probability (Softmax))

Let ϵ1,…,ϵm\epsilon_1, \ldots, \epsilon_mϵ1​,…,ϵm​ be i.i.d. Gumbel(μϵ,1/β)\mathrm{Gumbel}(\mu_\epsilon, 1/\beta)Gumbel(μϵ​,1/β) random variables. For any deterministic values x1,…,xm∈Rx_1, \ldots, x_m \in \mathbb{R}x1​,…,xm​∈R, the probability that index iii achieves the maximum is:

P(i∈argmax⁡j{xj+ϵj})=exp⁡(βxi)∑j=1mexp⁡(βxj)\mathbb{P}\left(i \in \operatorname{argmax}_j \{x_j + \epsilon_j\}\right) = \frac{\exp(\beta x_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^m \exp(\beta x_j)}P(i∈argmaxj​{xj​+ϵj​})=∑j=1m​exp(βxj​)exp(βxi​)​
(22)

This holds regardless of the location parameter μϵ\mu_\epsilonμϵ​.

Applying this result to our problem:

π(a∣s)=exp⁡(βxa(s))∑a′∈Asexp⁡(βxa′(s))=exp⁡(β(r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)v(j)))∑a′∈Asexp⁡(β(r(s,a′)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a′)v(j)))\pi(a|s) = \frac{\exp\left(\beta x_a(s)\right)}{\sum_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp\left(\beta x_{a'}(s)\right)} = \frac{\exp\left(\beta\left(r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a)v(j)\right)\right)}{\sum_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp\left(\beta\left(r(s,a') + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a')v(j)\right)\right)}π(a∣s)=∑a′∈As​​exp(βxa′​(s))exp(βxa​(s))​=∑a′∈As​​exp(β(r(s,a′)+γ∑j∈S​p(j∣s,a′)v(j)))exp(β(r(s,a)+γ∑j∈S​p(j∣s,a)v(j)))​
(23)

This is the softmax policy or Gibbs/Boltzmann policy with inverse temperature β\betaβ.

Properties:

  • As β→∞\beta \to \inftyβ→∞: the policy becomes deterministic, concentrating on the action(s) with highest xa(s)x_a(s)xa​(s) (recovers standard greedy policy)

  • As β→0\beta \to 0β→0: the policy becomes uniform over all actions (maximum entropy)

  • For finite β>0\beta > 0β>0: the policy is stochastic, with probability mass proportional to exponentiated Q-values

This completes the derivation: the smooth Bellman equation yields a value function v(s)v(s)v(s), and the corresponding optimal policy is the softmax over Q-values.

The Original and Augmented MDPs Side by Side¶

The derivation moves between two decision problems. The first is the original MDP solved with the smooth Bellman equation, or equivalently with an entropy bonus (Regularized Markov Decision Processes). The second is the augmented MDP, in which the decision maker solves a hard Bellman equation but sees a fresh shock on every action’s reward. The table puts them next to each other. We write q(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∑jp(j∣s,a) vβ⋆(j)q(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma\sum_{j} p(j\mid s,a)\, v^\star_\beta(j)q(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∑j​p(j∣s,a)vβ⋆​(j), which is the xa(s)x_a(s)xa​(s) of the derivation.

States∈Ss \in \mathcal{S}s∈S(s,ϵ)∈S×R∣As∣(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) \in \mathcal{S} \times \mathbb{R}^{\lvert\mathcal{A}_s\rvert}(s,ϵ)∈S×R∣As​∣
Noiseonly the transitions p(j∣s,a)p(j \mid s,a)p(j∣s,a)the transitions, plus a fresh i.i.d. Gumbel vector ϵt\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_tϵt​ each period
Reward of action aaar(s,a)r(s,a)r(s,a), plus the bonus β−1H(π(⋅∣s))\beta^{-1} H(\pi(\cdot \mid s))β−1H(π(⋅∣s))r(s,a)+ϵ(a)r(s,a) + \epsilon(a)r(s,a)+ϵ(a)

Optimal policystochastic, πβ(a∣s)∝exp⁡(βq(s,a))\pi_\beta(a \mid s) \propto \exp(\beta q(s,a))πβ​(a∣s)∝exp(βq(s,a))deterministic, σ(s,ϵ)=argmax⁡a{q(s,a)+ϵ(a)}\sigma(s,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \operatorname{argmax}_a \{q(s,a) + \epsilon(a)\}σ(s,ϵ)=argmaxa​{q(s,a)+ϵ(a)}

Who sees whatthe agent and the modeler both see sssthe agent sees sss and ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}ϵ; the modeler sees only sss

Figure 1 draws both problems as graphical models, one time slice after another.

The figure shows why the construction works. In panel (b), ϵt\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_tϵt​ has a single child, the action ata_tat​, and the action is a deterministic function of (st,ϵt)(s_t, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t)(st​,ϵt​). Integrating the shock out of slice ttt therefore changes only the conditional distribution of ata_tat​:

P(at=a∣st)=∫1{a=σ(st,ϵ)} g(ϵ) dϵ=πβ(a∣st),\mathbb{P}(a_t = a \mid s_t) = \int \mathbb{1}\{a = \sigma(s_t, \boldsymbol{\epsilon})\}\, g(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\, d\boldsymbol{\epsilon} = \pi_\beta(a \mid s_t),P(at​=a∣st​)=∫1{a=σ(st​,ϵ)}g(ϵ)dϵ=πβ​(a∣st​),
(24)

by Lemma 2. Doing this in every slice turns graph (b) into graph (a): the two models give the same distribution over state-action trajectories (s0,a0,s1,a1,…)(s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1, \ldots)(s0​,a0​,s1​,a1​,…). The missing arrows matter. If ϵt\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_tϵt​ also influenced st+1s_{t+1}st+1​, or if the shocks were correlated over time, integrating them out would leave a dependence on the past, and the marginal process would no longer be an MDP in sss. Rust (1987) states this as a conditional independence assumption, and his estimator relies on it.

The rewards are not equal path by path. The augmented agent collects r(st,at)+ϵt(at)r(s_t,a_t) + \epsilon_t(a_t)r(st​,at​)+ϵt​(at​), while the original MDP pays r(st,at)r(s_t,a_t)r(st​,at​) and the entropy bonus. They are equal on average. Conditional on which action wins, the winning value max⁡a{q(s,a)+ϵ(a)}\max_a\{q(s,a)+\epsilon(a)\}maxa​{q(s,a)+ϵ(a)} has the same distribution whatever the winner is, a property of the Gumbel distribution. Its mean is 1βlog⁡∑a′exp⁡(βq(s,a′))\frac{1}{\beta}\log\sum_{a'} \exp(\beta q(s,a'))β1​log∑a′​exp(βq(s,a′)) by Lemma 1, so

E[ϵ(a) ∣ σ(s,ϵ)=a]=1βlog⁡∑a′eβq(s,a′)−q(s,a)=−1βlog⁡πβ(a∣s).\mathbb{E}\big[\epsilon(a) \,\big|\, \sigma(s,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = a\big] = \frac{1}{\beta}\log\sum_{a'} e^{\beta q(s,a')} - q(s,a) = -\frac{1}{\beta}\log \pi_\beta(a \mid s).E[ϵ(a)∣∣​σ(s,ϵ)=a]=β1​loga′∑​eβq(s,a′)−q(s,a)=−β1​logπβ​(a∣s).
(25)

The shock that the agent collects on the action it picks is, on average, −1βlog⁡πβ(a∣s)-\frac{1}{\beta}\log\pi_\beta(a\mid s)−β1​logπβ​(a∣s). Averaging over a∼πβ(⋅∣s)a \sim \pi_\beta(\cdot\mid s)a∼πβ​(⋅∣s) gives 1βH(πβ(⋅∣s))\frac{1}{\beta}H(\pi_\beta(\cdot \mid s))β1​H(πβ​(⋅∣s)), the entropy bonus. The per-action penalty −αlog⁡π(a∣s)-\alpha \log \pi(a \mid s)−αlogπ(a∣s) that appears later in the regularized formulation is this expected shock, with α=1/β\alpha = 1/\betaα=1/β. A rarely chosen action is chosen only when its shock is large, and the entropy bonus is the average of those large shocks.

Checking the Equivalence Numerically¶

The augmented MDP is a device for theory: it explains where the log-sum-exp comes from and gives a likelihood for observed choices, but nobody solves it to compute a policy. On a small problem we can still solve it by brute force and check that it gives the same answer as the original MDP. The cell below draws a random MDP with 5 states and 3 actions, sets γ=0.9\gamma = 0.9γ=0.9 and β=2\beta = 2β=2, and computes the solution in three ways.

  1. Original MDP. Smooth value iteration with the log-sum-exp, then the softmax policy.

  2. Original MDP, regularized reading. The value of that softmax policy with its entropy bonus, from the linear system (I−γPπ)v=rπ+β−1Hπ(\mathbf{I}-\gamma\mathbf{P}_\pi)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{r}_\pi + \beta^{-1}\mathbf{H}_\pi(I−γPπ​)v=rπ​+β−1Hπ​.

  3. Augmented MDP. Value iteration with the hard max on the ex-ante value, v(s)←Eϵ[max⁡a{r(s,a)+γ∑jp(j∣s,a)v(j)+ϵ(a)}]v(s) \leftarrow \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}[\max_a\{r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_j p(j\mid s,a)v(j)+\epsilon(a)\}]v(s)←Eϵ​[maxa​{r(s,a)+γ∑j​p(j∣s,a)v(j)+ϵ(a)}], with the expectation replaced by an average over 50,000 Gumbel draws and no log-sum-exp anywhere. We then simulate 20,000 episodes in which the agent sees fresh shocks at every step, takes the deterministic action argmax⁡a{q(s,a)+ϵ(a)}\operatorname{argmax}_a\{q(s,a)+\epsilon(a)\}argmaxa​{q(s,a)+ϵ(a)}, and collects r+ϵ(a)r + \epsilon(a)r+ϵ(a).

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_states, n_actions, gamma, beta = 5, 3, 0.9, 2.0
P = rng.dirichlet(0.5 * np.ones(n_states), size=(n_states, n_actions))  # P[s, a, j]
r = rng.normal(size=(n_states, n_actions))
loc, scale = -np.euler_gamma / beta, 1 / beta  # mean-zero Gumbel shocks


def smooth_max(q):
    """(1/beta) log sum_a exp(beta q), computed stably along the last axis."""
    m = q.max(axis=-1)
    return m + np.log(np.exp(beta * (q - m[..., None])).sum(axis=-1)) / beta


# Original MDP: smooth value iteration, then the softmax policy.
v = np.zeros(n_states)
for _ in range(500):
    v = smooth_max(r + gamma * P @ v)
q = r + gamma * P @ v
pi = np.exp(beta * (q - v[:, None]))
entropy = -(pi * np.log(pi)).sum(axis=1)

# Original MDP, regularized reading: evaluate pi with its entropy bonus,
# (I - gamma P_pi) v = r_pi + H_pi / beta.
P_pi = np.einsum("sa,saj->sj", pi, P)
v_reg = np.linalg.solve(np.eye(n_states) - gamma * P_pi, (pi * r).sum(axis=1) + entropy / beta)

# Augmented MDP: hard Bellman equation, ex-ante value. The expectation over the
# current shocks is an average over n_draws fixed Gumbel draws; no log-sum-exp.
n_draws = 50_000
shocks = rng.gumbel(loc, scale, size=(n_draws, n_states, n_actions))
v_aug = np.zeros(n_states)
for _ in range(150):
    v_aug = (r + gamma * P @ v_aug + shocks).max(axis=2).mean(axis=0)
q_aug = r + gamma * P @ v_aug

# Simulate the augmented MDP: the agent sees fresh shocks every step and takes
# the deterministic action argmax_a q_aug(s, a) + eps(a).
n_episodes, horizon = 20_000, 150
s = np.zeros(n_episodes, dtype=int)
returns = np.zeros(n_episodes)
visits = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
shock_total = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
cdf = P.cumsum(axis=2)
for t in range(horizon):
    eps = rng.gumbel(loc, scale, size=(n_episodes, n_actions))
    a = (q_aug[s] + eps).argmax(axis=1)
    eps_a = eps[np.arange(n_episodes), a]
    returns += gamma**t * (r[s, a] + eps_a)
    np.add.at(visits, (s, a), 1)
    np.add.at(shock_total, (s, a), eps_a)
    s = (rng.random(n_episodes)[:, None] > cdf[s, a]).sum(axis=1)
freq = visits / visits.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
mean_shock = shock_total / visits

fmt = lambda x: " ".join(f"{y:6.3f}" for y in x)
lines = [
    "Values v(s)",
    f"  original, smooth value iteration        {fmt(v)}",
    f"  original, entropy-regularized eval      {fmt(v_reg)}",
    f"  augmented, hard max over Gumbel draws   {fmt(v_aug)}",
    f"  augmented, simulated return from s=0    {returns.mean():6.3f} +/- {2 * returns.std() / np.sqrt(n_episodes):.3f}",
    "",
    "Policy: softmax pi(a|s) vs. action frequencies of the augmented agent",
    "  s |  softmax pi(.|s)      |  frequency in augmented MDP",
]
lines += [f"  {i} | {fmt(pi[i])} | {fmt(freq[i])}" for i in range(n_states)]
lines += [
    "",
    "Shocks: -log pi(a|s)/beta vs. mean shock eps(a) when a is chosen",
    "  s |  -log pi(.|s)/beta    |  mean chosen shock",
]
lines += [f"  {i} | {fmt(-np.log(pi[i]) / beta)} | {fmt(mean_shock[i])}" for i in range(n_states)]
lines += [
    "",
    f"  entropy bonus H/beta per state     {fmt(entropy / beta)}",
    f"  mean chosen shock per state        {fmt(shock_total.sum(1) / visits.sum(1))}",
]
print("\n".join(lines))

  original, entropy-regularized eval      10.098 11.741 11.022 10.392 11.100

  augmented, simulated return from s=0    10.116 +/- 0.026

The three value functions agree up to Monte Carlo error, which stays below 0.01 on values near 10, and the simulated return of the augmented agent from state 0 matches vβ⋆(0)v^\star_\beta(0)vβ⋆​(0) within its confidence interval. The augmented agent never randomizes, yet the frequencies of its actions reproduce the softmax probabilities to the third decimal. The last two blocks check the shock identity: the mean shock on a chosen action matches −β−1log⁡πβ(a∣s)-\beta^{-1}\log\pi_\beta(a\mid s)−β−1logπβ​(a∣s), and its average per state matches the entropy bonus. The cost explains why the Gumbel route stays theoretical. One brute-force sweep evaluates 50,000×5×350{,}000 \times 5 \times 350,000×5×3 maxima, where the log-sum-exp needs 5×35 \times 35×3 exponentials, and the brute-force answer is still off in the third digit.

Regularized Markov Decision Processes¶

Which convex penalty on action distributions generates a desired smooth maximum through conjugate duality?

Regularized MDPs Geist et al. (2019) provide another perspective on how the smooth Bellman equations come to be. This framework offers a more general approach in which we seek to find optimal policies under the infinite horizon criterion while also accounting for a regularizer that influences the kind of policies we try to obtain.

Let’s set up some necessary notation. First, recall that the policy evaluation operator for a stationary policy with decision rule π\piπ is defined as:

Lπv=rπ+γPπv\BellmanPi \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{r}_\pi + \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi \mathbf{v}Lπ​v=rπ​+γPπ​v
(26)

where rπ\mathbf{r}_\pirπ​ is the expected reward vector under policy π\piπ, γ\gammaγ is the discount factor, and Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​ is the state transition probability matrix under π\piπ. A complementary object to the value function is the q-function (or Q-factor) representation:

qγπ(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)vγπ(j)vγπ(s)=∑a∈Asπ(a∣s)qγπ(s,a)\begin{align*} q_\gamma^{\pi}(s, a) &= r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v_\gamma^{\pi}(j) \\ v_\gamma^{\pi}(s) &= \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \pi(a | s) q_\gamma^{\pi}(s, a) \end{align*}qγπ​(s,a)vγπ​(s)​=r(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)vγπ​(j)=a∈As​∑​π(a∣s)qγπ​(s,a)​
(27)

The policy evaluation operator can then be written in terms of the q-function as:

[Lπv](s)=⟨π(⋅∣s),q(s,⋅)⟩[\BellmanPi v](s) = \langle \pi(\cdot | s), q(s, \cdot) \rangle[Lπ​v](s)=⟨π(⋅∣s),q(s,⋅)⟩
(28)

Legendre-Fenchel Transform¶

The workhorse behind the theory of regularized MDPs is the Legendre-Fenchel transform, also known as the convex conjugate. For a strongly convex function Ω:Δ(As)→R\Omega: \Delta(\mathcal{A}_s) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}Ω:Δ(As​)→R, its Legendre-Fenchel transform Ω∗:RAs→R\Omega^*: \mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{A}_s} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}Ω∗:RAs​→R is defined as:

Ω∗(q(s,⋅))=max⁡π(⋅∣s)∈Δ(As)⟨π(⋅∣s),q(s,⋅)⟩−Ω(π(⋅∣s))\Omega^*(q(s, \cdot)) = \max_{\pi(\cdot|s) \in \Delta(\mathcal{A}_s)} \langle \pi(\cdot | s), q(s, \cdot) \rangle - \Omega(\pi(\cdot | s))Ω∗(q(s,⋅))=π(⋅∣s)∈Δ(As​)max​⟨π(⋅∣s),q(s,⋅)⟩−Ω(π(⋅∣s))
(29)

An important property of this transform is that it has a unique maximizing argument, given by the gradient of Ω∗\Omega^*Ω∗:

∇Ω∗(q(s,⋅))=arg⁡max⁡π⟨π(⋅∣s),q(s,⋅)⟩−Ω(π(⋅∣s))\nabla \Omega^*(q(s, \cdot)) = \arg\max_\pi \langle \pi(\cdot | s), q(s, \cdot) \rangle - \Omega(\pi(\cdot | s))∇Ω∗(q(s,⋅))=argπmax​⟨π(⋅∣s),q(s,⋅)⟩−Ω(π(⋅∣s))
(30)

The gradient is also Lipschitz: if Ω\OmegaΩ is κ\kappaκ-strongly convex, a change of qqq moves the maximizing policy by at most 1/κ1/\kappa1/κ times as much. A more strongly convex regularizer therefore makes the policy less sensitive to errors in qqq. An important example of a regularizer is the negative entropy, which gives rise to the smooth Bellman equations as we are about to see. Scaled by the temperature 1/β1/\beta1/β, it is (1/β)(1/\beta)(1/β)-strongly convex, so the softmax policy moves by at most β\betaβ times the change in qqq (measuring qqq in the sup norm and policies in the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm).

Regularized Bellman Operators¶

How do the regularizer and its convex conjugate alter Bellman evaluation, policy improvement, and their contraction properties?

With these concepts in place, we can now define the regularized Bellman operators:

  1. Regularized Policy Evaluation Operator (Lπ,Ω)(\mathrm{L}_{\pi,\Omega})(Lπ,Ω​):

    [Lπ,Ωv](s)=⟨q(s,⋅),π(⋅∣s)⟩−Ω(π(⋅∣s))[\mathrm{L}_{\pi,\Omega} v](s) = \langle q(s,\cdot), \pi(\cdot | s) \rangle - \Omega(\pi(\cdot | s))[Lπ,Ω​v](s)=⟨q(s,⋅),π(⋅∣s)⟩−Ω(π(⋅∣s))
    (31)

  2. Regularized Bellman Optimality Operator (LΩ)(\mathrm{L}_\Omega)(LΩ​):

    [LΩv](s)=[max⁡πLπ,Ωv](s)=Ω∗(q(s,⋅))[\mathrm{L}_\Omega v](s) = [\max_\pi \mathrm{L}_{\pi,\Omega} v ](s) = \Omega^*(q(s, \cdot))[LΩ​v](s)=[πmax​Lπ,Ω​v](s)=Ω∗(q(s,⋅))
    (32)

It can be shown that the addition of a regularizer in these regularized operators still preserves the contraction properties, and therefore the existence of a solution to the optimality equations and the convergence of successive approximation.

The regularized value function of a stationary policy with decision rule π\piπ, denoted by vπ,Ωv_{\pi,\Omega}vπ,Ω​, is the unique fixed point of the operator equation:

find v such that v=Lπ,Ωv\text{find $v$ such that } \enspace v = \mathrm{L}_{\pi,\Omega} vfind v such that v=Lπ,Ω​v
(33)

Under the usual assumptions on the discount factor and the boundedness of the reward, the value of a policy can also be found in closed form by solving for v\mathbf{v}v in the linear system of equations:

(I−γPπ)v=rπ−Ωπ(\mathbf{I} - \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi) \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{r}_\pi - \boldsymbol{\Omega}_\pi(I−γPπ​)v=rπ​−Ωπ​
(34)

where [Ωπ](s)=Ω(π(⋅∣s))[\boldsymbol{\Omega}_\pi](s) = \Omega(\pi(\cdot|s))[Ωπ​](s)=Ω(π(⋅∣s)) is the vector of regularization terms at each state.

The associated state-action value function qπ,Ωq_{\pi,\Omega}qπ,Ω​ is given by:

qπ,Ω(s,a)=r(s,a)+∑j∈Sγp(j∣s,a)vπ,Ω(j)vπ,Ω(s)=∑a∈Asπ(a∣s)qπ,Ω(s,a)−Ω(π(⋅∣s))\begin{align*} q_{\pi,\Omega}(s, a) &= r(s, a) + \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} \gamma p(j|s,a) v_{\pi,\Omega}(j) \\ v_{\pi,\Omega}(s) &= \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \pi(a | s) q_{\pi,\Omega}(s, a) - \Omega(\pi(\cdot | s)) \end{align*}qπ,Ω​(s,a)vπ,Ω​(s)​=r(s,a)+j∈S∑​γp(j∣s,a)vπ,Ω​(j)=a∈As​∑​π(a∣s)qπ,Ω​(s,a)−Ω(π(⋅∣s))​
(35)

The regularized optimal value function vΩ∗v^*_\OmegavΩ∗​ is then the unique fixed point of LΩ\mathrm{L}_\OmegaLΩ​ in the fixed point equation:

find v such that v=LΩv\text{find $v$ such that } v = \mathrm{L}_\Omega vfind v such that v=LΩ​v
(36)

The associated state-action value function qΩ∗q^*_\OmegaqΩ∗​ is given by:

qΩ∗(s,a)=r(s,a)+∑j∈Sγp(j∣s,a)vΩ∗(j)vΩ∗(s)=Ω∗(qΩ∗(s,⋅))\begin{align*} q^*_\Omega(s, a) &= r(s, a) + \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} \gamma p(j|s,a) v^*_\Omega(j) \\ v^*_\Omega(s) &= \Omega^*(q^*_\Omega(s, \cdot))\end{align*}qΩ∗​(s,a)vΩ∗​(s)​=r(s,a)+j∈S∑​γp(j∣s,a)vΩ∗​(j)=Ω∗(qΩ∗​(s,⋅))​
(37)

An important result in the theory of regularized MDPs is that there exists a unique optimal regularized policy. Specifically, if πΩ∗\pi^*_\OmegaπΩ∗​ is a conserving decision rule (i.e., πΩ∗=arg⁡max⁡πLπ,ΩvΩ∗\pi^*_\Omega = \arg\max_\pi \mathrm{L}_{\pi,\Omega} v^*_\OmegaπΩ∗​=argmaxπ​Lπ,Ω​vΩ∗​), then the randomized stationary policy π=const(πΩ∗)\boldsymbol{\pi} = \mathrm{const}(\pi^*_\Omega)π=const(πΩ∗​) is the unique optimal regularized policy.

In practice, once we have found vΩ∗v^*_\OmegavΩ∗​, we can derive the optimal decision rule by taking the gradient of the convex conjugate evaluated at the optimal action-value function:

π∗(⋅∣s)=∇Ω∗(qΩ∗(s,⋅))\pi^*(\cdot | s) = \nabla \Omega^*(q^*_\Omega(s, \cdot))π∗(⋅∣s)=∇Ω∗(qΩ∗​(s,⋅))
(38)

Recovering the Smooth Bellman Equations¶

Under this framework, we can recover the smooth Bellman equations by choosing Ω\OmegaΩ to be the negative entropy scaled by the temperature 1/β1/\beta1/β, and obtain the softmax policy as the gradient of the convex conjugate. Let’s show this explicitly:

  1. Using the scaled negative entropy regularizer:

    Ω(π(⋅∣s))=1β∑a∈Asπ(a∣s)log⁡π(a∣s)\Omega(\pi(\cdot|s)) = \frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \pi(a|s) \log \pi(a|s)Ω(π(⋅∣s))=β1​a∈As​∑​π(a∣s)logπ(a∣s)
    (39)

  2. The convex conjugate:

    Ω∗(q(s,⋅))=1βlog⁡∑a∈Asexp⁡(βq(s,a))\Omega^*(q(s, \cdot)) = \frac{1}{\beta}\log \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp \big(\beta q(s,a)\big)Ω∗(q(s,⋅))=β1​loga∈As​∑​exp(βq(s,a))
    (40)

  3. Now, let’s write out the regularized Bellman optimality equation:

    vΩ∗(s)=Ω∗(qΩ∗(s,⋅))v^*_\Omega(s) = \Omega^*(q^*_\Omega(s, \cdot))vΩ∗​(s)=Ω∗(qΩ∗​(s,⋅))
    (41)

  4. Substituting the expressions for Ω∗\Omega^*Ω∗ and qΩ∗q^*_\OmegaqΩ∗​:

    vΩ∗(s)=1βlog⁡∑a∈Asexp⁡(β(r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)vΩ∗(j)))v^*_\Omega(s) = \frac{1}{\beta}\log \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp \left(\beta\Big(r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v^*_\Omega(j)\Big)\right)vΩ∗​(s)=β1​loga∈As​∑​exp⎝⎛​β(r(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)vΩ∗​(j))⎠⎞​
    (42)

This matches the form of the smooth Bellman equation we derived earlier, with the log-sum-exp operation replacing the max operation of the standard Bellman equation. With β=1\beta = 1β=1, the unscaled negative entropy gives the same equation at unit temperature.

Furthermore, the optimal policy is given by the gradient of Ω∗\Omega^*Ω∗:

π∗(a∣s)=∇Ω∗(qΩ∗(s,⋅))a=exp⁡(βqΩ∗(s,a))∑a′∈Asexp⁡(βqΩ∗(s,a′))\pi^*(a|s) = \nabla \Omega^*(q^*_\Omega(s, \cdot))_a = \frac{\exp(\beta q^*_\Omega(s,a))}{\sum_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp(\beta q^*_\Omega(s,a'))}π∗(a∣s)=∇Ω∗(qΩ∗​(s,⋅))a​=∑a′∈As​​exp(βqΩ∗​(s,a′))exp(βqΩ∗​(s,a))​
(43)

This is the familiar softmax policy we encountered in the smooth MDP setting.

Smooth Policy Iteration Algorithm¶

One identity links the log-sum-exp to the regularized evaluation operator. Let πq(⋅∣s)\pi_q(\cdot \mid s)πq​(⋅∣s) be the softmax of βq(s,⋅)\beta q(s,\cdot)βq(s,⋅). Then

1βlog⁡∑aexp⁡(βq(s,a))=∑aπq(a∣s) q(s,a)+1βH(πq(⋅∣s)),\frac{1}{\beta}\log\sum_{a} \exp\big(\beta q(s,a)\big) = \sum_a \pi_q(a \mid s)\, q(s,a) + \frac{1}{\beta} H\big(\pi_q(\cdot \mid s)\big),β1​loga∑​exp(βq(s,a))=a∑​πq​(a∣s)q(s,a)+β1​H(πq​(⋅∣s)),
(44)

which one checks by substituting log⁡πq(a∣s)=βq(s,a)−log⁡∑a′exp⁡(βq(s,a′))\log \pi_q(a \mid s) = \beta q(s,a) - \log\sum_{a'} \exp(\beta q(s,a'))logπq​(a∣s)=βq(s,a)−log∑a′​exp(βq(s,a′)) into the entropy. Line 6 of Algorithm 1 can therefore be written as “form the softmax policy, then add its expected qqq and its entropy bonus”. Algorithms stated that way are sometimes called entropy-regularized value iteration, but they are smooth value iteration with the log-sum-exp expanded. Policy iteration is different: it evaluates each policy completely before improving it.

Algorithm 2 (Smooth Policy Iteration)

Input: MDP (S,A,r,p,γ)(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, r, p, \gamma)(S,A,r,p,γ), inverse temperature β>0\beta > 0β>0, tolerance ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0

Output: Stochastic policy π\piπ, ε\varepsilonε-optimal for the entropy-regularized objective, and its value vvv

  1. Initialize π(a∣s)←1/∣As∣\pi(a|s) \leftarrow 1/|\mathcal{A}_s|π(a∣s)←1/∣As​∣ for all s∈Ss \in \mathcal{S}s∈S, a∈Asa \in \mathcal{A}_sa∈As​ (uniform policy)

  2. repeat

  3. \quad Evaluation: solve (I−γPπ)v=rπ+1βHπ(\mathbf{I} - \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{r}_\pi + \frac{1}{\beta}\mathbf{H}_\pi(I−γPπ​)v=rπ​+β1​Hπ​, where [rπ](s)=∑aπ(a∣s)r(s,a)[\mathbf{r}_\pi](s) = \sum_a \pi(a|s) r(s,a)[rπ​](s)=∑a​π(a∣s)r(s,a) and [Hπ](s)=−∑aπ(a∣s)log⁡π(a∣s)[\mathbf{H}_\pi](s) = -\sum_a \pi(a|s)\log\pi(a|s)[Hπ​](s)=−∑a​π(a∣s)logπ(a∣s)

  4. q(s,a)←r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)v(j)\quad q(s,a) \leftarrow r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v(j)q(s,a)←r(s,a)+γ∑j∈S​p(j∣s,a)v(j) for all s∈Ss \in \mathcal{S}s∈S, a∈Asa \in \mathcal{A}_sa∈As​

  5. Δ←max⁡s∈S(1βlog⁡∑a∈Asexp⁡(βq(s,a))−v(s))\quad \Delta \leftarrow \max_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \big(\frac{1}{\beta}\log\sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s}\exp(\beta q(s,a)) - v(s)\big)Δ←maxs∈S​(β1​log∑a∈As​​exp(βq(s,a))−v(s)), the Bellman residual ∥Lβv−v∥∞\|\mathrm{L}_\beta v - v\|_\infty∥Lβ​v−v∥∞​

  6. \quad if Δ<ε(1−γ)\Delta < \varepsilon(1-\gamma)Δ<ε(1−γ) then return v,πv, \piv,π

  7. \quad Improvement: π(a∣s)←exp⁡(βq(s,a))∑a′∈Asexp⁡(βq(s,a′))\pi(a|s) \leftarrow \frac{\exp(\beta q(s,a))}{\sum_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp(\beta q(s,a'))}π(a∣s)←∑a′∈As​​exp(βq(s,a′))exp(βq(s,a))​ for all s∈Ss \in \mathcal{S}s∈S, a∈Asa \in \mathcal{A}_sa∈As​

Properties of smooth policy iteration:

  1. Entropy-regularized evaluation. Line 3 is the linear system for the regularized value vπ,Ωv_{\pi,\Omega}vπ,Ω​ of Regularized Bellman Operators, with the entropy vector Hπ\mathbf{H}_\piHπ​ on the right-hand side. Replacing the exact solve by a few sweeps of v←rπ+1βHπ+γPπvv \leftarrow \mathbf{r}_\pi + \frac{1}{\beta}\mathbf{H}_\pi + \gamma\mathbf{P}_\pi vv←rπ​+β1​Hπ​+γPπ​v gives the smooth version of Algorithm 4.

  2. Stochastic improvement. Line 7 uses the softmax instead of the argmax. As β→∞\beta \to \inftyβ→∞ the method recovers standard policy iteration, and lower β\betaβ gives policies with more entropy. As in the hard case, the improvement does not need to be applied in every state for the method to make progress. The policy-iteration loops hidden inside actor-critic methods make use of this.

  3. What the stopping rule guarantees. The residual in line 5 is nonnegative, because vvv is the regularized value of π\piπ and the softmax maximizes the regularized one-step objective, so Lβv≥Lπ,Ωv=v\mathrm{L}_\beta v \ge \mathrm{L}_{\pi,\Omega} v = vLβ​v≥Lπ,Ω​v=v. For any vvv, the triangle inequality and the contraction property give ∥v−vβ⋆∥∞≤∥v−Lβv∥∞+γ∥v−vβ⋆∥∞\|v - v^\star_\beta\|_\infty \le \|v - \mathrm{L}_\beta v\|_\infty + \gamma\|v - v^\star_\beta\|_\infty∥v−vβ⋆​∥∞​≤∥v−Lβ​v∥∞​+γ∥v−vβ⋆​∥∞​, so

    ∥v−vβ⋆∥∞≤∥Lβv−v∥∞1−γ.\|v - v^\star_\beta\|_\infty \le \frac{\|\mathrm{L}_\beta v - v\|_\infty}{1-\gamma}.∥v−vβ⋆​∥∞​≤1−γ∥Lβ​v−v∥∞​​.
    (45)

    This is the a posteriori bound of Theorem 3 written for one step of Lβ\mathrm{L}_\betaLβ​ from vvv. Since vvv is the exact regularized value of the current π\piπ, the test of line 6 guarantees that π\piπ itself is within ε\varepsilonε of the optimal regularized value in every state. A test on the change of the policy, such as ∥π−πold∥<ε\|\pi - \pi_{\text{old}}\| < \varepsilon∥π−πold​∥<ε, would give no such guarantee.

  4. Convergence. The algorithm converges to the unique optimal regularized value function and policy. Unlike standard policy iteration, it does not terminate after finitely many iterations: the softmax policies form a continuum and the iterates approach the optimum without reaching it, which is why the loop stops on a tolerance. The convergence is fast, since each iteration is a Newton step (Smooth Policy Iteration Is Newton’s Method).

Smooth Policy Iteration Is Newton’s Method¶

The link between policy iteration and the Newton-Kantorovich method (Newton-Kantorovich and Policy Iteration) is easier to see here than in the hard case, because Lβ\mathrm{L}_\betaLβ​ is differentiable everywhere and there are no ties to worry about. The derivative of the log-sum-exp with respect to its arguments is the softmax, so the Fréchet derivative of Lβ\mathrm{L}_\betaLβ​ at vvv is

Lβ′(v)=γPπv,πv(a∣s)=exp⁡(βqv(s,a))∑a′exp⁡(βqv(s,a′)),qv(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∑jp(j∣s,a)v(j),\mathrm{L}_\beta'(v) = \gamma \mathbf{P}_{\pi_v}, \qquad \pi_v(a \mid s) = \frac{\exp(\beta q_v(s,a))}{\sum_{a'}\exp(\beta q_v(s,a'))}, \quad q_v(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma\sum_j p(j\mid s,a) v(j),Lβ′​(v)=γPπv​​,πv​(a∣s)=∑a′​exp(βqv​(s,a′))exp(βqv​(s,a))​,qv​(s,a)=r(s,a)+γj∑​p(j∣s,a)v(j),
(46)

the transition matrix of the softmax policy. A Newton step on v−Lβv=0v - \mathrm{L}_\beta v = 0v−Lβ​v=0 solves

(I−γPπv) vnew=Lβv−γPπvv.(\mathbf{I} - \gamma\mathbf{P}_{\pi_v})\, v_{\text{new}} = \mathrm{L}_\beta v - \gamma\mathbf{P}_{\pi_v} v.(I−γPπv​​)vnew​=Lβ​v−γPπv​​v.
(47)

At the softmax policy the log-sum-exp equals the expected qqq plus the entropy bonus, Lβv=rπv+γPπvv+1βHπv\mathrm{L}_\beta v = \mathbf{r}_{\pi_v} + \gamma\mathbf{P}_{\pi_v} v + \frac{1}{\beta}\mathbf{H}_{\pi_v}Lβ​v=rπv​​+γPπv​​v+β1​Hπv​​. The right-hand side is therefore rπv+1βHπv\mathbf{r}_{\pi_v} + \frac{1}{\beta}\mathbf{H}_{\pi_v}rπv​​+β1​Hπv​​, and the Newton step is exactly the entropy-regularized evaluation of the softmax policy. Smooth policy iteration is the Newton-Kantorovich method applied to the smooth Bellman equation, without the semismooth machinery that the hard max requires.

Rust (1987) solved his smooth Bellman equation this way. He did not call it policy iteration. He recognized an operator equation, a root-finding problem in a function space, and applied Newton-Kantorovich to it, after a few rounds of successive approximation to get close enough for Newton’s method to converge quickly.

Equivalence Between Smooth Bellman Equations and Entropy-Regularized MDPs¶

We have now seen three ways to arrive at the smooth Bellman equation: as a smoothed maximum, from Gumbel noise on the rewards, and as the optimality equation of a regularized MDP. It is worth writing the third one as an optimization problem over policies, because that is the form used by maximum entropy RL. With entropy weight α=1/β\alpha = 1/\betaα=1/β, the entropy-regularized MDP is

max⁡π  Eπ[∑t=0∞γt(r(st,at)+αH(π(⋅∣st)))],H(π(⋅∣s))=−∑aπ(a∣s)log⁡π(a∣s).\max_\pi\; \mathbb{E}_\pi \left[ \sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t \Big( r(s_t, a_t) + \alpha H\big(\pi(\cdot|s_t)\big) \Big) \right], \qquad H(\pi(\cdot|s)) = -\sum_a \pi(a|s) \log \pi(a|s).πmax​Eπ​[t=0∑∞​γt(r(st​,at​)+αH(π(⋅∣st​)))],H(π(⋅∣s))=−a∑​π(a∣s)logπ(a∣s).
(48)

Since H(π(⋅∣s))=Ea∼π(⋅∣s)[−log⁡π(a∣s)]H(\pi(\cdot|s)) = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi(\cdot|s)}[-\log \pi(a|s)]H(π(⋅∣s))=Ea∼π(⋅∣s)​[−logπ(a∣s)], the entropy bonus in state sss is the average of a per-action term, and the objective equals

Eπ[∑t=0∞γt(r(st,at)−αlog⁡π(at∣st))].\mathbb{E}_\pi \left[ \sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t \big( r(s_t, a_t) - \alpha \log \pi(a_t|s_t) \big) \right].Eπ​[t=0∑∞​γt(r(st​,at​)−αlogπ(at​∣st​))].
(49)

Entropy regularization therefore amounts to paying −αlog⁡π(a∣s)-\alpha\log\pi(a|s)−αlogπ(a∣s) for taking action aaa, a cost that is high for actions the policy rarely takes. This is the form that sample-based methods such as soft actor-critic estimate, since it only needs the probability of the action that was taken. In the augmented MDP of The Original and Augmented MDPs Side by Side, the same quantity is the expected shock on the chosen action.

The Bellman optimality equation of this problem maximizes, in each state, over the distribution π(⋅∣s)\pi(\cdot|s)π(⋅∣s):

v(s)=max⁡π(⋅∣s)∈Δ(As)∑aπ(a∣s)(q(s,a)−αlog⁡π(a∣s)),q(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a) v(j).v(s) = \max_{\pi(\cdot|s) \in \Delta(\mathcal{A}_s)} \sum_a \pi(a|s) \big( q(s,a) - \alpha \log \pi(a|s) \big), \qquad q(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a)\, v(j).v(s)=π(⋅∣s)∈Δ(As​)max​a∑​π(a∣s)(q(s,a)−αlogπ(a∣s)),q(s,a)=r(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)v(j).
(50)

The inner problem is the convex conjugate of the scaled negative entropy, which we computed in “Recovering the Smooth Bellman Equations”. A direct check is also short. Writing πq\pi_qπq​ for the softmax of βq(s,⋅)\beta q(s,\cdot)βq(s,⋅), for any distribution π\piπ,

∑aπ(a∣s)(q(s,a)−αlog⁡π(a∣s))=αlog⁡∑aexp⁡(q(s,a)/α)−α KL(π(⋅∣s) ∥ πq(⋅∣s)),\sum_a \pi(a|s) \big( q(s,a) - \alpha \log \pi(a|s) \big) = \alpha \log\sum_a \exp\big(q(s,a)/\alpha\big) - \alpha\, \mathrm{KL}\big(\pi(\cdot|s) \,\big\|\, \pi_q(\cdot|s)\big),a∑​π(a∣s)(q(s,a)−αlogπ(a∣s))=αloga∑​exp(q(s,a)/α)−αKL(π(⋅∣s)∥∥​πq​(⋅∣s)),
(51)

and the KL divergence is nonnegative and zero only at π=πq\pi = \pi_qπ=πq​. The maximum is the log-sum-exp with β=1/α\beta = 1/\alphaβ=1/α, attained by the softmax policy. So the value function that solves the smooth Bellman equation is the optimal value of the entropy-regularized MDP, and the softmax policy is its optimal policy. The two descriptions differ only in how they present the problem: as smoothing the Bellman operator, or as trading off reward against policy entropy. Maximum entropy RL algorithms such as soft actor-critic use both, the smooth operator for its differentiability and the regularized objective to explain why the policy should stay stochastic.

Continuous Action and State Spaces¶

What changes in the smooth Bellman equation when the sums over actions become integrals?

So far the action sets were finite. In control problems the action is usually a vector a∈As⊆Rma \in \mathcal{A}_s \subseteq \mathbb{R}^ma∈As​⊆Rm, a torque, a dose, a flow rate, and the state is often continuous too. The smooth Bellman equation carries over once we fix a reference measure μ\muμ on the actions. For a finite set, μ\muμ is the counting measure and integrals against it are sums. For a box or another bounded subset of Rm\mathbb{R}^mRm, it is usually the Lebesgue measure dadada. It can also be a probability measure, a prior policy π0(da∣s)\pi_0(da \mid s)π0​(da∣s). This is the continuous version of the Legendre-Fenchel pair (negative entropy, log-sum-exp), and in statistical physics it is called the Gibbs variational principle.

The reference measure matters. With a finite action set, relabeling the actions changes nothing. With continuous actions, the entropy depends on μ\muμ, and that dependence shows up in three ways.

  • Prior policies give KL regularization. If μ=π0(⋅∣s)\mu = \pi_0(\cdot \mid s)μ=π0​(⋅∣s) is a probability measure, then ∫νlog⁡ν dμ=KL(ν ∥ π0)\int \nu \log \nu\, d\mu = \mathrm{KL}(\nu \,\|\, \pi_0)∫νlogνdμ=KL(ν∥π0​) and the problem is KL-regularized RL: the agent is penalized for moving away from π0\pi_0π0​. In the finite case, the uniform prior gives KL(ν ∥ uniform)=log⁡∣As∣−H(ν)\mathrm{KL}(\nu\,\|\,\text{uniform}) = \log\lvert\mathcal{A}_s\rvert - H(\nu)KL(ν∥uniform)=log∣As​∣−H(ν), so entropy and KL regularization differ by a constant per state and have the same optimal policy.

  • Differential entropy has no floor. Under the Lebesgue measure, h(π)=−∫πlog⁡π dah(\pi) = -\int \pi \log \pi\, dah(π)=−∫πlogπda is the differential entropy, which is negative for concentrated densities: a Gaussian with variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 in one dimension has h=12log⁡(2πeσ2)h = \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e \sigma^2)h=21​log(2πeσ2), negative once σ2<1/(2πe)\sigma^2 < 1/(2\pi e)σ2<1/(2πe). It also depends on the units of the action. Rescaling a↦c aa \mapsto c\,aa↦ca in Rm\mathbb{R}^mRm adds mlog⁡∣c∣m \log\lvert c\rvertmlog∣c∣ to hhh. That only shifts all values by a constant and leaves the policy unchanged, but a nonlinear change of variables, say from a torque to its logarithm, changes the optimal policy.

  • Unbounded action sets need care. If As=Rm\mathcal{A}_s = \mathbb{R}^mAs​=Rm with the Lebesgue measure and bounded rewards, the integral diverges and the smooth Bellman equation has no solution. The remedies are a bounded action set (soft actor-critic squashes its Gaussian samples through a tanh⁡\tanhtanh into a box), a prior policy as reference measure, or rewards that decrease fast enough in ∥a∥\lVert a\rVert∥a∥, such as a quadratic action cost.

The regularization adds exploration noise around the LQR controller, more of it along the directions where the cost is flat, and does not change the gain.

Gumbel shocks over a continuum. The augmented-MDP construction needs one shock per action. Over a continuum of actions we cannot attach independent shocks to every point, since the supremum of uncountably many independent Gumbel variables is infinite. The replacement is a Gumbel process Maddison et al. (2014): a random function GGG on As\mathcal{A}_sAs​ such that, for every measurable set BBB, the maximum max⁡a∈BG(a)\max_{a \in B} G(a)maxa∈B​G(a) is Gumbel with location log⁡μ(B)\log\mu(B)logμ(B) and unit scale, independently over disjoint sets. For such a process, max⁡a{βq(s,a)+G(a)}\max_a\{\beta q(s,a) + G(a)\}maxa​{βq(s,a)+G(a)} is Gumbel with location log⁡∫eβq(s,a)μ(da)\log\int e^{\beta q(s,a)}\mu(da)log∫eβq(s,a)μ(da), and its argmax has the Gibbs density. With ϵt=Gt/β\epsilon_t = G_t/\betaϵt​=Gt​/β the derivation of Gumbel Noise on the Rewards goes through with a random function in place of a random vector, and Figure 1 still describes the model. It is even less a computational object than in the finite case. Maddison et al. (2014) use it to build an exact sampler, A* sampling, but the algorithms for continuous control, soft actor-critic among them, work with the Gibbs density directly and approximate it with a parametric policy.

Rust’s Bus Engines and Inverse Reinforcement Learning¶

What can we learn about a decision maker’s goals from records of what they did?

Rust’s 1987 paper is worth reading for three reasons: it contains the smooth Bellman equation, it poses what is now called inverse reinforcement learning, and it solves that problem with a bilevel method that relies on implicit differentiation, a tool that became popular in machine learning three decades later for hyperparameter optimization.

The problem. Harold Zurcher was the superintendent of maintenance at the Madison Metropolitan bus company. Rust had his maintenance records: for each bus, the odometer reading each month, and the months in which Zurcher replaced the engine. Replacing an engine is expensive, while keeping an old engine running costs more and more as the mileage grows. The question was how Zurcher decided when to replace. Rust is a structural econometrician. Structural econometrics does not stop at predicting behavior; it posits a mechanism that generates it, here a decision maker solving an MDP, and fits the parameters of that mechanism to data. The fitted mechanism can then answer questions the data alone cannot, such as how behavior would change if the price of an engine changed.

The model. The state sss is the mileage since the last replacement, discretized into bins. Each month there are two actions, keep (a=0a=0a=0) or replace (a=1a=1a=1). Keeping costs c(s;θ)c(s;\theta)c(s;θ), increasing in sss; replacing costs a fixed amount RCRCRC and resets the mileage. With parameters θ\thetaθ collecting RCRCRC and those of ccc, the reward is rθ(s,0)=−c(s;θ)r_\theta(s,0) = -c(s;\theta)rθ​(s,0)=−c(s;θ) and rθ(s,1)=−RC−c(0;θ)r_\theta(s,1) = -RC - c(0;\theta)rθ​(s,1)=−RC−c(0;θ), and the mileage transitions are estimated directly from the odometer data. The data contradict any deterministic policy: two buses with the same mileage are sometimes treated differently. Rust’s answer was the Gumbel model of Gumbel Noise on the Rewards. Zurcher sees, in addition to sss, a shock ϵ(a)\epsilon(a)ϵ(a) for each action that the econometrician does not see, and acts optimally given both. Integrating out the shocks gives the smooth Bellman equation and the softmax choice probabilities

vθ=Lβ,θ vθ,πθ(a∣s)=exp⁡(βqθ(s,a))∑a′exp⁡(βqθ(s,a′)).v_\theta = \mathrm{L}_{\beta,\theta}\, v_\theta, \qquad \pi_\theta(a \mid s) = \frac{\exp(\beta q_\theta(s,a))}{\sum_{a'}\exp(\beta q_\theta(s,a'))}.vθ​=Lβ,θ​vθ​,πθ​(a∣s)=∑a′​exp(βqθ​(s,a′))exp(βqθ​(s,a))​.
(55)

This is the second, deeper reason Rust used these equations. Besides being smooth, they follow from the random-utility models of McFadden (1974), the standard statistical basis of discrete choice in econometrics, in the same way that least squares follows from assuming Gaussian noise. In machine learning terms, McFadden’s conditional logit is multiclass logistic regression with a structural interpretation.

The estimator. Given observed pairs (st,at)(s_t, a_t)(st​,at​), maximize the log-likelihood ℓ(θ)=∑tlog⁡πθ(at∣st)\ell(\theta) = \sum_t \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)ℓ(θ)=∑t​logπθ​(at​∣st​). Every evaluation of ℓ\ellℓ requires solving the smooth Bellman equation for the current θ\thetaθ, so the problem is bilevel: an outer maximization over θ\thetaθ around an inner fixed-point problem. Rust called his algorithm the nested fixed point (NFXP) algorithm. The gradient of ℓ\ellℓ needs ∂vθ/∂θ\partial v_\theta / \partial\theta∂vθ​/∂θ, which the implicit function theorem provides without differentiating through the iterations of the inner solver. Differentiating vθ=Lβ,θvθv_\theta = \mathrm{L}_{\beta,\theta} v_\thetavθ​=Lβ,θ​vθ​ and using the derivative of Lβ\mathrm{L}_\betaLβ​ from Smooth Policy Iteration Is Newton’s Method,

∂vθ∂θ=(I−γPπθ)−1 ∂rπθ∂θ,∂rπθ∂θ(s)=∑aπθ(a∣s) ∂rθ(s,a)∂θ.\frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial \theta} = (\mathbf{I} - \gamma\mathbf{P}_{\pi_\theta})^{-1}\, \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_{\pi_\theta}}{\partial\theta}, \qquad \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_{\pi_\theta}}{\partial\theta}(s) = \sum_a \pi_\theta(a\mid s)\, \frac{\partial r_\theta(s,a)}{\partial \theta}.∂θ∂vθ​​=(I−γPπθ​​)−1∂θ∂rπθ​​​,∂θ∂rπθ​​​(s)=a∑​πθ​(a∣s)∂θ∂rθ​(s,a)​.
(56)

The matrix to invert is the one of policy evaluation, already factored by the Newton steps of the inner solver. For rewards linear in the parameters, rθ(s,a)=θ⊤ϕ(s,a)r_\theta(s,a) = \theta^\top\phi(s,a)rθ​(s,a)=θ⊤ϕ(s,a), this derivative is the vector of expected discounted feature counts under the softmax policy, the quantity that Ziebart et al. (2008) matches to the empirical feature counts. The score of one observation is then

∇θlog⁡πθ(a∣s)=β(∇θqθ(s,a)−∑a′πθ(a′∣s) ∇θqθ(s,a′)),∇θqθ(s,a)=∇θrθ(s,a)+γ∑jp(j∣s,a) ∂vθ∂θ(j).\nabla_\theta \log\pi_\theta(a\mid s) = \beta\Big(\nabla_\theta q_\theta(s,a) - \sum_{a'}\pi_\theta(a'\mid s)\,\nabla_\theta q_\theta(s,a')\Big), \qquad \nabla_\theta q_\theta(s,a) = \nabla_\theta r_\theta(s,a) + \gamma\sum_j p(j\mid s,a)\,\frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial \theta}(j).∇θ​logπθ​(a∣s)=β(∇θ​qθ​(s,a)−a′∑​πθ​(a′∣s)∇θ​qθ​(s,a′)),∇θ​qθ​(s,a)=∇θ​rθ​(s,a)+γj∑​p(j∣s,a)∂θ∂vθ​​(j).
(57)
Algorithm 3 (Nested Fixed Point (NFXP) Maximum Likelihood)

Input: Observed state-action pairs {(st,at)}\{(s_t, a_t)\}{(st​,at​)}, transition model ppp, discount γ\gammaγ, scale β\betaβ, initial parameters θ0\theta_0θ0​
Output: Estimated reward parameters θ^\hat\thetaθ^

  1. repeat for k=0,1,…k = 0, 1, \ldotsk=0,1,…

    1. (Inner problem) Solve v=Lβ,θkvv = \mathrm{L}_{\beta,\theta_k} vv=Lβ,θk​​v: a few sweeps of Algorithm 1, then Newton steps (Smooth Policy Iteration Is Newton’s Method), warm-started from the previous vvv

    2. Compute πθk\pi_{\theta_k}πθk​​, qθkq_{\theta_k}qθk​​ and ∂vθk/∂θ\partial v_{\theta_k}/\partial\theta∂vθk​​/∂θ by the implicit-function formula above

    3. Compute ∇ℓ(θk)=∑t∇θlog⁡πθk(at∣st)\nabla \ell(\theta_k) = \sum_t \nabla_\theta\log\pi_{\theta_k}(a_t\mid s_t)∇ℓ(θk​)=∑t​∇θ​logπθk​​(at​∣st​)

    4. (Outer step) θk+1←θk+Hk−1∇ℓ(θk)\theta_{k+1} \leftarrow \theta_k + H_k^{-1}\nabla\ell(\theta_k)θk+1​←θk​+Hk−1​∇ℓ(θk​), with HkH_kHk​ a positive definite curvature estimate (Rust used the outer product of the scores, the BHHH method)

  2. until ∥∇ℓ(θk)∥\|\nabla\ell(\theta_k)\|∥∇ℓ(θk​)∥ is small

  3. return θ^=θk\hat\theta = \theta_kθ^=θk​

What the model assumes. The setup is a strong one, and naming its assumptions explains why inverse RL is hard in general.

  • Rationality. The decision maker is assumed to solve the MDP exactly. People do not; the literature on bounded rationality studies how they fall short, and Rust himself has written skeptically about whether people follow Bellman’s principle of optimality. The assumption is still a useful starting point, in the same way a linear model is.

  • Observability. Rust observes the state and the action. In many applications one or both are missing. With logged prices, for instance, an unchanged price may be a decision to keep it or simply the absence of a decision, and the action itself must be inferred, which makes the problem partially observable.

  • Identifiability. Many reward functions explain the same behavior equally well. With hard maxima, a constant reward makes every policy optimal, and adding a shaping term γΦ(s′)−Φ(s)\gamma\Phi(s') - \Phi(s)γΦ(s′)−Φ(s) to any reward leaves the optimal policies unchanged Ng et al. (1999). The map from rewards to behavior is many-to-one, so the data can at best single out a set of candidate rewards. Structural econometrics restores identification by restricting the reward to a parametric family, fixing the discount factor and the scale β\betaβ, and normalizing one action’s reward. Whether such restrictions are acceptable depends on the goal: predicting what Zurcher would do under new engine prices is a weaker demand than recovering what he “really” wanted.

Summary and Outlook¶

Entropy regularization replaces hard action selection with a smooth conjugate operator and produces a stochastic optimal policy. Gumbel perturbations, log-sum-exp Bellman updates, and regularized policy iteration describe the same construction from probabilistic, variational, and algorithmic viewpoints. Drawn as graphical models, the original MDP and the Gumbel-augmented MDP differ by one shock node per time step, and integrating it out recovers the softmax policy; the expected shock on the chosen action is the entropy bonus. The same equations hold for continuous actions once a reference measure is fixed, with integrals in place of sums and a Gibbs density in place of the softmax, and the choice of that measure becomes part of the model. Smooth policy iteration is Newton’s method on the smooth Bellman equation, and Rust’s nested fixed-point estimator uses the same derivative to recover reward parameters from observed behavior.

The same log-sum-exp form appears over whole trajectories in continuous time. Path-integral stochastic control examines systems driven by Gaussian disturbances whose Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation becomes linear under a logarithmic transformation, so that optimal feedback can be estimated from weighted trajectories.

Smoothness changes the operator but does not remove the need to represent its unknown value function. How can an infinite-dimensional functional equation be reduced to finitely many coefficients and test conditions? Weighted-residual methods provide the general approximation machinery.

Self-checks¶

Exercise 1 (Temperature limit)

What happens to a softmax policy as the entropy temperature α\alphaα approaches zero, assuming a unique maximizing action?

Solution to Exercise 1

Its probability concentrates on the maximizing action, so the soft policy approaches the ordinary greedy deterministic policy.

Exercise 2 (Smooth maximum)

Why is log-sum-exp often easier to optimize through than a hard maximum?

Solution to Exercise 2

Log-sum-exp is differentiable and blends information from all actions. A hard maximum is nondifferentiable at ties and passes local gradient information only through selected maximizers.

Exercise 3 (Entropy as an expected shock)

In the augmented MDP the agent never randomizes. Where does the entropy bonus of the original MDP come from in its rewards?

Solution to Exercise 3

From the shocks on the actions it picks. Given that action aaa wins, its shock has mean −1βlog⁡πβ(a∣s)-\frac{1}{\beta}\log\pi_\beta(a\mid s)−β1​logπβ​(a∣s), which is large for actions that rarely win. Averaging over the winning action gives 1βH(πβ(⋅∣s))\frac{1}{\beta}H(\pi_\beta(\cdot\mid s))β1​H(πβ​(⋅∣s)), the entropy bonus.

Exercise 4 (Units of a continuous action)

A one-dimensional action is measured in newton-metres, and you switch to kilonewton-metres. What happens to the entropy-regularized optimal value and policy under the Lebesgue reference measure? What if you switch to the logarithm of the torque?

Solution to Exercise 4

Dividing the action by 1000 subtracts log⁡1000\log 1000log1000 from the differential entropy of every density, so every value shifts by the constant −log⁡1000β(1−γ)-\frac{\log 1000}{\beta(1-\gamma)}−β(1−γ)log1000​ and the policy, mapped back to newton-metres, is unchanged. A logarithmic change of variables is nonlinear: the Lebesgue measure in the new variable is a different measure on torques, so the regularizer and the optimal policy both change.
